newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW-NZ GDP confirms slowdown, no surprise.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-NZ GDP confirms slowdown, no surprise.

text.p: Following are economists' initial reactions to New Zealand June quarter GDP data released on Friday.

Real seasonally-adjusted production-based GDP rose 0.3 percent in the quarter and 2.1 percent seasonally-adjusted from the year ago quarter, versus consensus forecasts of 0.4 percent and 1.8 percent respectively.
"I think the production-based series is pretty much in line with expectations, so further evidence that the economy is slowing but still a reasonable rate of growth -- the economy is not collapsing.
"I think (we) still place greater reliance on the production-based figure, but the expenditure-based one was a bit weaker.
"No significant impact (on currency and rates). I think the GDP data is fairly historical anyway and not significantly out of line with expectation, so no implications for monetary policy."
"It's pretty much in line with what we expected, but I think some of the sector groups are perhaps a bit weaker than we expected.
"Manufacturing and construction, two big parts of the economy, they're into negative for the first time for some time.

"I think this result would be in line with the Reserve Bank's expectations and the scenario that they've been painting. "I think it does confirm to some extent the slowdown in the economy -- it's not across the board by any stretch, but I think
it does fit their (the RBNZ's) scenario and I don't think it brings forward or pushes out when monetary policy may be able to be eased."
Graham said the surprise was the upward revision to 0.7 percent from 0.4 percent for March quarter production-based GDP, which made the slowdown between March and June stronger than expected.
Otherwise the figures were in line with expectations.
"The growth path is coming down," Graham said.
He said the data were not market-moving as they were largely historical and did not take account of tax cuts which took effect on July 1.
"What the Reserve Bank is concerned about is where we're at now and where we're going. The June quarter is very historical."
